web_evidence.title: Violín — Fragmento | Penguin Libros
web_evidence.note: Opened authorized publisher excerpt of the Spanish translation. The proem identifies the account as the narrator’s own life, tragedy, and triumph, and the sustained opening chapter has Triana narrate her actions, memories, home, and Karl’s death as yo/me/mi.

web_evidence.title: Violin by Anne Rice | PenguinRandomHouse.com
web_evidence.note: Publisher page identifies the complete novel and reproduces a Cleveland Plain Dealer description that the tale is told from Triana’s point of view; its synopsis follows Triana and Stefan through the climax.

web_evidence.title: Violin by Anne Rice | Publishers Weekly
web_evidence.note: The full-book review explicitly identifies Triana as the narrator, describes her distinctive voice, and follows her through Stefan’s past and her later return to the present and journey to Brazil.

web_evidence.title: Musical Madness Played on Unusual Stradivarius — “Violin” Review
web_evidence.note: Contemporary St. Louis Post-Dispatch review explicitly calls Triana the narrator and discusses how her narration changes in style as the book progresses.

web_evidence.title: ‘Violin’ A Great Read | The Spokesman-Review
web_evidence.note: Contemporary Dallas Morning News review explicitly calls Triana Rice’s narrator and describes her narration of her name, family history, Stefan’s past, and the later struggle over the violin.

person_note: Triana is the participating controlling narrator. Numerous independent quote passages expose her as “I” across memories, observation, performance, grief, and family history. The Tier A publisher excerpt independently establishes sustained first-person self-narration in the proem and opening chapter, while several contemporary whole-book reviews explicitly identify Triana as narrator and trace that voice through later Vienna and Brazil material. Third-person references to Stefan are objects of Triana’s narration, not evidence of a nonparticipating narrator; dialogue, aphorisms, and the voice implied by music are local material. The authorized excerpt is opening-scoped, but the interior quote sample and multiple whole-book descriptions extend the evidence beyond it. No credible evidence of sustained narration in another person was found.
